title: Thirteen Weeks Out: Why October Is the Right Time to Bring In Fractional CFO Support Before Christmas
excerpt: Christmas trading and the January lull it's followed by are thirteen weeks away. Here's why the window to have a cash view ready for both closes long before December does.
content:
By the last week of October, most owner-led businesses on the East Coast are past the EOFY admin and well into a different kind of thinking: what spring and early summer trade is going to look like, and how stretched the team will be by the time Christmas trading peaks. It's also, without most owners noticing, the exact point in the calendar where the window to get ahead of the next three months starts to close.

Thirteen weeks from today lands in the third week of January. That stretch covers the two biggest swings most Australian SMEs will feel this financial year: the cash tied up in stock, casual wages and marketing ahead of Christmas trading, and the quieter, often expensive lull that follows once the decorations come down. Most businesses live through both as separate surprises. A fractional CFO partnership that starts now treats them as one connected forecast instead.

This isn't a pitch for urgency. It's a pattern we see across owner-led businesses every year: the decision to bring in financial leadership gets made reactively, usually once the cash position is already tight or a lender has asked a question nobody can answer quickly. Timing it by the calendar, rather than by crisis, changes what the next three months actually look like.

Why the Calendar Matters More Than the Crisis

Most fractional CFO engagements start the same way: something has already gone wrong, or growth has outpaced the finance function's ability to keep up. Both are legitimate reasons to call for support. But they share one disadvantage, which is that by the time the decision gets made, the lead time to actually prepare for what's coming has usually already been spent.

Christmas trading is a known quantity. So is the quieter trading that typically follows it into late January. The businesses that handle both periods well aren't the ones with the biggest pipeline or the deepest pockets, they're the ones who had visibility into the cash position before the swing started, not partway through it. Nothing about either period is a surprise on the calendar, only in how most businesses choose to meet it.

What the First Few Weeks of a Fractional CFO Partnership Actually Build

Bringing in a fractional CFO partnership is not an instant fix. The first few weeks are spent understanding the ledger, reconciling how the business actually makes money against how the reports say it does, and building the first real view of where cash sits week by week. For a lot of our clients, that first deliverable looks a lot like the 13-Week Cash Flow Build, a rolling forecast that gets rebuilt weekly rather than a static annual budget nobody revisits after March.

Starting that process now, in late October, means the forecast is live and tested well before Christmas trading begins, rather than assembled in a hurry once the first supplier invoice lands earlier than expected. It also means any gaps in the underlying numbers, a supplier account that's never reconciled cleanly, a payroll on-cost that's been under-recorded for months, surface while there's still time to fix them before they matter.

The Two Swings a Thirteen-Week View Actually Covers

The first swing is obvious: stock, casual wages and marketing spend all tend to land before the Christmas revenue does, which is exactly the kind of timing mismatch that makes a profitable quarter feel like a cash-poor one. The second swing gets less attention. January is traditionally quiet for a lot of East Coast SMEs, trading slows, staff are back from leave, and the usual run of BAS, superannuation and lease commitments doesn't pause just because revenue has.

A single rolling forecast that runs through both periods, rather than two separate ad hoc guesses made weeks apart, is the difference between reacting to each swing and already knowing what each one is going to do to the bank balance. That kind of cash flow discipline is hard to build retrospectively once the quiet month has already landed, because by then the forecast is describing a problem that's already happened rather than one that's still avoidable.

You Don't Need a Reason to Start Now

None of this requires the business to be in trouble. The owners who get the most value out of starting a fractional CFO partnership in October aren't usually the ones in crisis, they're the ones who'd rather spend the next thirteen weeks working from a plan than finding out what Christmas and January actually cost them after the fact.

That's a different kind of decision to the one most owners expect to make about financial support, and it's one worth making before the calendar makes it for you.

faqs.q: What is the right time of year to bring in a fractional CFO for an Australian SME?
faqs.a: There's no single right time, but late October gives a thirteen-week run into the quieter part of January, covering both Christmas trading and the slow start to the new year. Starting a fractional CFO partnership before both swings land means the forecast is already built and tested, rather than assembled in a hurry once the first supplier bill arrives.

faqs.q: How long does it take to onboard a fractional CFO partnership?
faqs.a: The first few weeks are typically spent understanding the ledger, reconciling how the business reports its numbers against how it actually makes money, and building a rolling cash flow view the team can keep running. It isn't an overnight fix, which is exactly why starting before a known busy period, rather than during one, matters most to the businesses that do it.

faqs.q: How much does a fractional CFO cost for a small or medium business in Australia?
faqs.a: Cost depends on the tier of support and how often the CFO is involved, from a monthly management pack through to weekly involvement in lender and leadership conversations. The fractional CFO cost guide breaks down what drives the price up or down for different business sizes and stages of growth.

faqs.q: Why is a rolling cash flow forecast better than an annual budget before Christmas trading?
faqs.a: An annual budget is usually set once and rarely revisited, while a rolling forecast is rebuilt weekly against what's actually happening in the bank account. Ahead of Christmas trading, when stock and wage spending lands well before the revenue does, that weekly view is what shows the cash gap coming before it arrives rather than after.

faqs.q: Do I need to already be in financial trouble to bring in a fractional CFO?
faqs.a: No. The pattern we see across owner-led businesses is that the decision gets made reactively far more often than it needs to. Businesses that bring in fractional CFO support before a known busy period tend to use it to plan ahead rather than to recover from something that's already happened to the cash position.

faqs.q: What actually happens financially to most businesses in January after Christmas trading?
faqs.a: Trading typically slows, staff return from leave, and recurring costs like BAS, superannuation and lease payments don't pause just because revenue has. Businesses that feel this as a shock usually haven't modelled it; a cash flow forecast built in advance turns the quiet month into something expected rather than a fresh surprise each year.

faqs.q: Can a fractional CFO partnership start partway through the financial year?
faqs.a: Yes. A fractional CFO partnership isn't tied to the financial year calendar, it starts whenever the business needs the visibility. Starting in October simply means the first forecast lands before Christmas trading rather than during the busiest weeks of it, when there's far less room to act on what it shows.
